extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for school teachers on how to train pupils' thinking: what intellectual habits to cultivate, which school conditions and methods help or hinder reflective thought, and how to select and organize subject-matter and activities to produce orderly, significant, and logical thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on significant features (not trivial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions of the pupil's contact with subject-matter may be such that he is compelled to come to quarters with its more significant features, or such that he is encouraged to deal with it upon the basis of what is trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assumptions that one thought is as good as another or that the end of study is merely the amassing of information; design learning situations that force discrimination between significant and meaningless aspects of subject-matter rather than rewarding mere verbal connections among words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of mind: value depth over mere promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes slowness and depth of response are intimately connected. Time is required in order to digest impressions, and translate them into substantial ideas. 'Brightness' may be but a flash in the pan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Afford pupils time and leisure to gather forces and avoid rebuking slowness when it reflects deeper processing; resist teaching habits that encourage speedy snapshot judgments for the sake of recitation or displays of memorized information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize individual differences in modes of thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking is specific, not a machine-like, ready-made apparatus to be turned indifferently and at will upon all subjects...different things suggest their own appropriate meanings, tell their own unique stories, and in that they do this in very different ways with different persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should study individual traits and not judge intelligence solely by prompt answers or by conformity to a teacher's favored method; selection of methods should be adapted to varied natural modes of approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any subject can be intellectual (thinking is functional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any subject, from Greek to cooking, and from drawing to mathematics, is intellectual, if intellectual at all, not in its fixed inner structure, but in its function--in its power to start and direct significant inquiry and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not presume some subjects are inherently 'intellectual'; instead evaluate and choose subject-matter by its capacity to provoke curiosity, inquiry, and the logical organization of material for particular pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orderliness/continuity of thought requires organization of suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts...and conclusions suggested by them...do not constitute reflective thought. The suggestions must be organized; they must be arranged with reference to one another and with reference to the facts on which they depend for proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate consecutiveness (flexibility and variety of materials conjoined with singleness and definiteness of direction); avoid both mechanical routine uniformity and a grasshopper-like scattering of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration as a steady unified trend (not fixity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration does not mean fixity, nor a cramped arrest or paralysis of the flow of suggestion. It means variety and change of ideas combined into a single steady trend moving toward a unified conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach pupils to keep ideas moving toward an object (unity of direction) rather than suppress variation; consistent thinking permits varied and even incompatible suggestions provided each is related to the main topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical demands and organized activity foster orderly thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual organization originates and for a time grows as an accompaniment of the organization of the acts required to realize an end...The need of thinking to accomplish something beyond thinking is more potent than thinking for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use occupational or goal-directed activities (even simplified for children) to provide continuous axes around which knowledge and inference habits can be organized; test inferences by results achieved to discourage futile scattering methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select educative activities with threefold criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem...is discovering and arranging the forms of activity (a) which are most congenial, best adapted, to the immature stage of development; (b) which have the most ulterior promise as preparation for the social responsibilities of adult life; and (c) which, at the same time, have the maximum of influence in forming habits of acute observation and of consecutive inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing school activities choose those that are developmentally appropriate, preparatory for adult functions, and potent in forming habits of observation and orderly inference; avoid activities that are merely entertaining or merely adult-like imitations without educative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid oscillation between neglecting and overvaluing activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational practice shows a continual tendency to oscillate between two extremes...One extreme is to neglect them almost entirely...The other extreme is an enthusiastic belief in the almost magical educative efficacy of any kind of activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject both extremes: do not discard overt activity as chaotic, nor assume any spontaneous activity will automatically foster mental training; instead select and shape activities deliberately to serve intellectual ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method includes unconscious environmental and personal influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Method covers not only what [the teacher] intentionally devises and employs for the purpose of mental training, but also what he does without any conscious reference to it,--anything in the atmosphere and conduct of the school which reacts in any way upon the curiosity, the responsiveness, and the orderly activity of children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the whole school atmosphere and the teacher's unexamined habits shape pupils' intellectual attitudes; cultivate constructive personal habits and deliberately arrange the environment to support curiosity and orderly activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example and stimulus-response: teacher habits powerfully condition pupils
rubrics_metrics.description: Example is more potent than precept...Everything the teacher does, as well as the manner in which he does it, incites the child to respond in some way or other, and each response tends to set the child's attitude in some way or other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and adjust one's personal manner, speech, tone, and implicit standards because pupils fuse the teacher's personality with the subject and respond toward or away from it; small unconscious habits can have large intellectual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers unconsciously judge others by their own mental habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Most persons are quite unaware of the distinguishing peculiarities of their own mental habit. They take their own mental operations for granted, and unconsciously make them the standard for judging the mental processes of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imposing the teacher's own cognitive preferences (e.g., theoretic interest vs executive ability) as universal norms; actively seek to recognize and support diverse intellectual proclivities among pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting teacher-personality for subject-matter as motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers...tend to rely upon their personal strong points to hold a child to his work, and thereby to substitute their personal influence for that of subject-matter as a motive for study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal influence sparingly and ensure pupils' relation to subject-matter—not merely to the teacher—is primary, lest dependence on the teacher weaken pupils' intrinsic engagement with topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster independent thinking rather than answering to please teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: The operation of the teacher's own mental habit tends...to make the child a student of the teacher's peculiarities rather than of the subjects that he is supposed to study. 'Is this right?' comes to mean 'Will this answer or this process satisfy the teacher?' instead of 'Does it satisfy the inherent conditions of the problem?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage pupils to evaluate answers against the inherent conditions of problems; design tasks and assessment so that correctness is judged by problem-solution quality, not by conformity to teacher expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary (abstract) studies risk isolation from life
rubrics_metrics.description: In the so-called disciplinary or pre-eminently logical studies, there is danger of the isolation of intellectual activity from the ordinary affairs of life...The abstract tends to become so aloof...as to be cut loose from practical and moral bearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect abstract subjects to concrete applications and moral/practical contexts to prevent theoretic specialization that fails to transfer to ordinary life and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill-based studies risk mechanical drill and loss of reflective acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: In subjects where the main emphasis is upon acquisition of skill...the tendency is to take the shortest cuts possible to gain the required end. This makes the subjects mechanical, and thus restrictive of intellectual power...Sheer imitation, dictation of steps to be taken, mechanical drill, may give results most quickly and yet strengthen traits likely to be fatal to reflective power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure skills are acquired with intelligence—provide reasons, opportunities for reflective practice, and understanding during acquisition so technique can later be used intelligently rather than as rote automaticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational studies risk amassing facts without wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is knowledge which is merely acquired and stored up; wisdom is knowledge operating in the direction of powers to the better living of life...In school, amassing information always tends to escape from the ideal of wisdom or good judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach information as integral to problem-solving and thinking processes: acquire facts through their use in thinking and inference so that knowledge becomes serviceable rather than a mere heap of memorized items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid valuing external results (correct answer) above intellectual process
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal of the product, as against that of the mental process by which the product is attained...manifests itself in the importance attached to the 'correct answer.' As long as this end is uppermost...training of mind remains an incidental and secondary consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluation and school organization to reward process, inquiry, explanation, and reasoning as well as correct results; beware of administrative pressures (exams, marks, promotions) that privilege rapid, demonstrable external results over the development of habits of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical thinking as careful, thorough, and practical reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: In its practical sense logical is synonymous with wide-awake, thorough, and careful reflection...Caution, carefulness, thoroughness, definiteness, exactness, orderliness, methodic arrangement, are, then, the traits by which we mark off the logical from what is random and casual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orient intellectual education toward forming the logical disposition—habits of careful scrutiny, weighing, relating things definitely, and systematic method—rather than toward formal abstractions divorced from thoughtful practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate psychological tendencies with logical training (avoid two false schools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two opposing schools err: one makes the 'natural' primary and slight of intellectual nurture; the other relies upon subject-matter and external discipline to import logical habits into a reluctant mind. Both neglect the intrinsic connections between psychological tendencies and logical achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt methods that cultivate native curiosity and individual attitudes while also organizing subject-matter so pupils learn to apply and internalize logical habits; avoid purely laissez-faire 'natural' methods and also avoid treating logic as mere external conformity through rote definitions and classifications.
